summary: A long-acting benzodiazepine used mainly to treat alcohol withdrawal and short-term anxiety, but with important risks of dependence, withdrawal, and overdose—especially when combined with opioids, alcohol, or other sedatives.
description: Chlordiazepoxide is one of the earliest benzodiazepines, introduced around 1960. It calms the nervous system and can reduce anxiety and alcohol withdrawal symptoms. Because it stays in the body a long time and has active metabolites, it can be very effective for withdrawal but also carries a higher risk of oversedation, falls, and accumulation in older adults or people with liver problems. Modern guidelines generally reserve it for specific situations (like alcohol withdrawal) and encourage short-term, lowest-effective-dose use when it is prescribed for anxiety.
patient_summary: Chlordiazepoxide is a calming medicine in the benzodiazepine family. It can help with anxiety and is commonly used in hospitals or detox programs to manage alcohol withdrawal. Like other benzodiazepines, it can make you sleepy, dizzy, and unsteady, and it can be habit-forming. Stopping it suddenly after regular use may trigger withdrawal symptoms, some of which can be serious. The risks are much higher if it’s taken with opioids, alcohol, or other drugs that cause drowsiness. For these reasons, chlordiazepoxide is usually used for short periods and under close medical supervision.

primary.condition_name: Short-term treatment of anxiety disorders or severe anxiety symptoms

secondary.context: Used to manage withdrawal symptoms when stopping or cutting down heavy alcohol use.
Sometimes used temporarily while longer-term treatments (like SSRIs) take effect.

therapeutic_response.display: Calming and sedating effects often begin within the first hour after a dose.

common_adverse_effects.notes: Most people feel at least somewhat sleepy. Plan activities so you don’t need to drive or make important decisions until you know how it affects you.
Getting up slowly and using support when walking can help prevent falls, especially in older adults.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Common with higher or ongoing doses
common_adverse_effects.notes: You may notice difficulty remembering new information or feeling mentally ‘slower’ while on the medication.

serious_risks.risk: Severe allergic reactions with rash, swelling, or difficulty breathing.
Severe confusion, agitation, paradoxical aggression, or dramatic behavior changes.
Signs of liver injury: yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, severe fatigue, or upper right abdominal pain.
Signs of bone marrow problems: frequent infections, fever, unusual bruising or bleeding, or extreme fatigue.
Marked drowsiness, very slow or shallow breathing, or inability to wake fully—especially if taken with opioids, alcohol, or other sedatives.
Withdrawal symptoms (anxiety, tremors, sweating, insomnia, hallucinations, seizures) if the drug is stopped abruptly after prolonged use.

black_box_warning: Benzodiazepines plus opioids: Using chlordiazepoxide together with opioid medications (like oxycodone, codeine, or morphine) or with illicit opioids can lead to profound sedation, slow or stopped breathing, coma, and death. This combination should only be used if there are no safer options, at the lowest effective doses, and with close monitoring.

Abuse, misuse, and addiction: Chlordiazepoxide, like other benzodiazepines, can be misused for its calming or sedating effects. Misuse often involves combining it with alcohol or other drugs, which raises the risk of overdose and death. People with a history of substance use should be monitored very closely or offered alternative treatments.

Dependence and withdrawal: Regular use can lead to physical dependence. Stopping suddenly or cutting the dose too quickly after ongoing use can trigger severe withdrawal symptoms (anxiety, tremor, agitation, hallucinations, seizures) that can be life-threatening. Chlordiazepoxide must be tapered slowly under medical guidance.

contraindications.contraindication: Allergy to chlordiazepoxide or any ingredient in the product
Breastfeeding (not recommended due to long half-life and risk of infant sedation/withdrawal)
History of serious benzodiazepine misuse or high risk of substance use disorder (relative contraindication; requires extreme caution)
Severe respiratory disease or sleep apnea where further respiratory depression would be dangerous (relative/clinical contraindication)
Severe liver dysfunction (use only with great caution, if at all)

precautions: Can cause significant drowsiness and slow reaction time—driving, operating machinery, or performing tasks that require full alertness can be dangerous.
In older adults, benzodiazepines are linked to confusion, delirium, falls, fractures, and car accidents; they also clear more slowly from the body.
People with breathing problems (such as COPD or sleep apnea) are at greater risk of respiratory depression.
Because the drug is metabolized in the liver and has long-acting metabolites, people with liver disease may experience prolonged and unpredictable sedation.
Paradoxical reactions can occur—some people, especially children, older adults, or those with certain psychiatric conditions, may become more agitated, disinhibited, or aggressive instead of calmer.

interactions.interactant: Opioid pain medicines and cough syrups (eg, oxycodone, hydrocodone, codeine, morphine, methadone, illicit opioids)
interactions.mechanism: Very high risk of life-threatening respiratory depression, coma, and death.
interactions.action: Avoid combination whenever possible. If absolutely necessary, use the lowest possible doses for the shortest time with close monitoring.

interactions.mechanism: Strong additive sedative effect, greatly increasing the risk of overdose, falls, and accidents.
interactions.action: Avoid alcohol completely while taking this medication.

interactions.interactant: Other benzodiazepines, sleep medicines, certain antipsychotics, sedating antidepressants, antihistamines, or muscle relaxants
interactions.mechanism: Additive sedation and impaired coordination, increasing risk of falls, confusion, and breathing problems.
interactions.action: Avoid overlapping sedatives unless specifically coordinated by your prescriber.

interactions.interactant: Drugs affecting liver enzymes (especially certain strong CYP3A4 inhibitors or inducers)
interactions.mechanism: May change how much chlordiazepoxide or its metabolites build up, altering sedation level and side effect risk.
interactions.action: Your prescriber or pharmacist should review your full medication list for interactions and adjust doses if needed.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Breathing and heart function: Watch for slow or shallow breathing, especially if the patient is also taking opioids or has lung disease.
Blood pressure and pulse, especially when starting or increasing doses or during alcohol withdrawal management.
Mental status: Look for confusion, excessive sedation, or paradoxical agitation or aggression.
Fall risk: Pay attention to balance, gait, and history of falls, particularly in older adults.
Withdrawal symptoms: When tapering, watch for return of anxiety, tremors, sweating, sleep problems, mood swings, hallucinations, or seizures.
Laboratory tests: If used long-term or if there are symptoms suggestive of blood or liver problems, periodic blood counts and liver function tests may be recommended.

special_populations.pregnancy: Chlordiazepoxide crosses the placenta. Use in pregnancy has been linked to possible birth defects in some studies (though data are mixed) and may cause sedation or withdrawal in the newborn, especially when used later in pregnancy. On the other hand, untreated severe anxiety and alcohol withdrawal can also be dangerous for both parent and baby. Decisions about use during pregnancy should be made carefully with a specialist, weighing all risks and benefits. Short-term use for alcohol withdrawal in a hospital setting may be appropriate.
special_populations.lactation: Benzodiazepines, including chlordiazepoxide, pass into breast milk. Because chlordiazepoxide is long-acting and can build up in the infant, there is a risk of sedation, poor feeding, and withdrawal symptoms. Safer, shorter-acting benzodiazepines are generally preferred if a benzodiazepine is needed while breastfeeding. In many cases, non-benzodiazepine approaches to anxiety are better choices.
special_populations.pediatric: Younger patients are more prone to paradoxical reactions (agitation, disinhibition) and to oversedation. Long-acting benzodiazepines are usually avoided unless there is a very clear benefit and close monitoring.
special_populations.geriatric: Older adults metabolize benzodiazepines more slowly and are more sensitive to their effects. Even standard doses can cause confusion, daytime sedation, falls, fractures, and worsened memory. Guidelines generally recommend avoiding long-acting benzodiazepines like chlordiazepoxide in this age group except for specific uses such as withdrawal management.
special_populations.renal_impairment: Severe kidney impairment can affect how the drug and its metabolites are cleared. Lower doses and careful monitoring are generally recommended.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Significant liver disease slows metabolism and increases the risk of prolonged sedation, confusion, and drug accumulation. Alternative benzodiazepines with simpler metabolism (or non-benzodiazepine strategies) are often preferred.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Well absorbed by mouth; peak blood levels reached within about 0.5–2 hours.
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Parent drug roughly 24–48 hours; active metabolites can last from many hours to several days.
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Processed in the liver into several active metabolites, including desmethyldiazepam and demoxepam, which have long half-lives.
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Mainly excreted in the urine as metabolites.

dosing.titration: Exact dosing must be individualized, especially in alcohol withdrawal and in people who are older or medically fragile. Never adjust your own dose without talking to your prescriber.

sections.heading: What It’s Used For
sections.text: Chlordiazepoxide is not a general-purpose ‘calming pill’ and should not be used casually. It’s reserved for specific situations where its benefits outweigh its risks.
items: Alcohol withdrawal syndrome: Helps prevent and treat shaking, anxiety, agitation, and seizures when someone with heavy alcohol use is stopping or cutting back. It is often part of a structured detox plan in hospital or supervised outpatient care.

Anxiety disorders: May be used short-term for significant anxiety while longer-term treatments (like SSRIs or therapy) are starting to work. Long-term daily use is generally discouraged due to dependence, withdrawal, and cognitive side-effects.
off_label: Occasional use in other anxiety-related conditions when first-line treatments are ineffective or not tolerated, under specialist supervision.

sections.heading: What It Feels Like

quotes: Many people notice less tension and anxiety within an hour or so.
Some feel pleasantly relaxed; others feel heavily sedated and foggy.
Because it’s long-acting, grogginess can last into the next day, especially at higher doses.
You may feel light-headed, dizzy, or unsteady on your feet.
Reaction time and concentration can be slower, which affects driving and fine motor tasks.
Older adults often feel more wobbly and are at higher risk for falls and fractures.
Some people describe feeling emotionally ‘numb’ or less engaged.
Memory for events that happen while under the influence can be patchy (anterograde amnesia).

sections.intro: People’s experiences with chlordiazepoxide vary depending on the dose, how long they’ve been taking it, and whether they’re withdrawing from alcohol.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works and How Long It Lasts
key_points: Effects can start within 30–60 minutes after an oral dose.
Calming and sedative effects may last many hours, especially as the drug and its metabolites build up.

Because it’s long-acting, chlordiazepoxide is useful for alcohol withdrawal (it smooths out ups and downs) but increases the risk of oversedation, especially in older adults and people with liver problems.
If taken regularly, the drug can accumulate over several days, which means side effects may increase over time even without raising the dose.

sections.heading: Major Safety Warnings
sections.highlight: Chlordiazepoxide is a controlled substance (C-IV). It can cause dependence, serious withdrawal, and life-threatening breathing problems, especially when mixed with opioids, alcohol, or other sedating drugs.
black_box: Benzodiazepines plus opioids: Using chlordiazepoxide together with opioid medications (like oxycodone, codeine, or morphine) or with illicit opioids can lead to profound sedation, slow or stopped breathing, coma, and death. This combination should only be used if there are no safer options, at the lowest effective doses, and with close monitoring.

Abuse, misuse, and addiction: Chlordiazepoxide, like other benzodiazepines, can be misused for its calming or sedating effects. Misuse often involves combining it with alcohol or other drugs, which raises the risk of overdose and death. People with a history of substance use should be monitored very closely or offered alternative treatments.

Dependence and withdrawal: Regular use can lead to physical dependence. Stopping suddenly or cutting the dose too quickly after ongoing use can trigger severe withdrawal symptoms (anxiety, tremor, agitation, hallucinations, seizures) that can be life-threatening. Chlordiazepoxide must be tapered slowly under medical guidance.
other: Can cause significant drowsiness and slow reaction time—driving, operating machinery, or performing tasks that require full alertness can be dangerous.
In older adults, benzodiazepines are linked to confusion, delirium, falls, fractures, and car accidents; they also clear more slowly from the body.
People with breathing problems (such as COPD or sleep apnea) are at greater risk of respiratory depression.
Because the drug is metabolized in the liver and has long-acting metabolites, people with liver disease may experience prolonged and unpredictable sedation.
Paradoxical reactions can occur—some people, especially children, older adults, or those with certain psychiatric conditions, may become more agitated, disinhibited, or aggressive instead of calmer.
patient_counseling: Never mix chlordiazepoxide with alcohol, opioids, or other sedating medications unless your doctor has specifically told you to—and even then, you must be closely monitored.
Use the smallest dose for the shortest possible time. This lowers the risk of dependence, memory problems, and falls.
Do not stop the medication suddenly if you’ve been taking it regularly for more than a couple of weeks. Talk to your prescriber about a gradual taper.
If you notice extreme sleepiness, slow or shallow breathing, or if someone cannot stay awake or respond normally after taking this medicine, call emergency services immediately.
Store it in a safe place, out of reach of children and where others cannot access it—misuse by friends or family can be very dangerous.

sections.heading: Possible Side Effects
sections.summary: Many side effects are related to its calming effect on the brain and body. While mild drowsiness is common, serious problems like falls, confusion, and breathing issues can occur, especially at higher doses or with other sedating medicines.
plain_language_list: Changes in mood, including feeling flat or disinhibited
Changes in libido or menstrual cycles (less common)
Blood problems (like very low white cells) and liver issues (rare but serious)

sections.intro: Chlordiazepoxide depresses the central nervous system, so combining it with other sedating or psychoactive substances greatly increases risks.

sections.heading: Dosing Overview
sections.text: Exact dosing must be individualized, especially in alcohol withdrawal and in people who are older or medically fragile. Never adjust your own dose without talking to your prescriber.

adult.alcohol_withdrawal: Dose is typically titrated based on withdrawal severity using a scale such as CIWA. Short courses usually last several days, with higher doses early on and a gradual decrease as symptoms improve.
adult.anxiety: Common total daily doses range from 10–40 mg divided into 2–4 doses per day, using the lowest dose that provides relief. Maximum usual daily dose is around 100 mg/day, but chronic high-dose use is discouraged.
adult.kidney_impairment: Mild to moderate impairment: often no change is needed. Very severe impairment or dialysis: some clinicians reduce the dose by about half due to slower clearance.
adult.liver_impairment: Because the drug is metabolized in the liver and has long-acting metabolites, people with liver disease are at higher risk of accumulation and oversedation. Starting doses should be low, with slow titration, and in some cases other benzodiazepines with simpler metabolism may be preferred.
adult.older_adult: Benzodiazepines are generally avoided in adults 65+ unless there is a strong indication (eg, alcohol withdrawal). If used, start at very low doses (eg, 5 mg 2–4 times daily for anxiety) and titrate slowly, with frequent reassessment of need.

pediatric.anxiety: In children 6 years and older, low doses (eg, 5 mg 2–4 times daily) may be used and carefully increased in select cases. However, newer medications are usually preferred for long-term anxiety treatment, and use in children is specialized and cautious.
pediatric.note: Chlordiazepoxide is not recommended for children under 6 years of age. Even in older children, any use should be supervised by a specialist.

sections.simple_explanation: For both anxiety and alcohol withdrawal, chlordiazepoxide is meant to be a short-term tool, not a long-term solution. The dose should be as low as possible for the shortest possible time, and any plan to stop it should include a gradual taper.

sections.heading: Monitoring and Safety Checks
items: Breathing and heart function: Watch for slow or shallow breathing, especially if the patient is also taking opioids or has lung disease.
Blood pressure and pulse, especially when starting or increasing doses or during alcohol withdrawal management.
Mental status: Look for confusion, excessive sedation, or paradoxical agitation or aggression.

Withdrawal symptoms: When tapering, watch for return of anxiety, tremors, sweating, sleep problems, mood swings, hallucinations, or seizures.

sections.heading: Available Forms
items: Oral capsules (5 mg, 10 mg, 25 mg) as the hydrochloride salt in both the US and Canada.
Available as multiple generics; usually dispensed as capsules for oral use.
Always check your specific product’s instructions and strength—do not assume all capsules are the same.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.text: Chlordiazepoxide is a benzodiazepine. It attaches to benzodiazepine sites on GABA-A receptors in the brain. GABA is the main ‘brake’ chemical for the nervous system. By enhancing GABA’s effect, chlordiazepoxide makes brain cells less excitable, which reduces anxiety, calms agitation, and can prevent seizures in alcohol withdrawal. The same calming effect, however, can also lead to drowsiness, slowed thinking, and slower breathing—especially when combined with other sedating substances.

sections.heading: Where It Fits in Modern Practice
sections.text: Chlordiazepoxide played a major role in early anxiolytic treatment after its introduction around 1960. Today, long-acting benzodiazepines are used more cautiously. For anxiety disorders, antidepressants (like SSRIs/SNRIs), psychotherapy (especially CBT), and lifestyle interventions are preferred for long-term management. Chlordiazepoxide is now used most often for alcohol withdrawal, where its long-lasting calming and anti-seizure effects are useful if carefully monitored. When it is used for anxiety, it is usually short term and part of a broader plan that includes safer long-term treatments.

faqs.a: Chlordiazepoxide is mainly used to manage symptoms of alcohol withdrawal and, less commonly, for short-term relief of significant anxiety. It is not usually a first-line or long-term treatment for anxiety because of its risk of dependence, withdrawal, and cognitive side effects.

Yes. Like all benzodiazepines, chlordiazepoxide can cause physical dependence and can be misused. Taking it regularly for more than a few weeks increases the risk of dependence. Stopping suddenly after regular use can cause withdrawal symptoms, including anxiety, insomnia, tremors, and in severe cases, seizures. It should always be tapered slowly under medical supervision.

faqs.q: How long should I take chlordiazepoxide for anxiety?
faqs.a: In most cases, chlordiazepoxide should only be used for short periods (usually a few weeks) while longer-term treatments, such as antidepressants or therapy, begin to work. If you have been taking it for longer, do not stop on your own—work with your prescriber on a gradual tapering plan.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking chlordiazepoxide?
faqs.a: No. Mixing chlordiazepoxide with alcohol greatly increases the risk of dangerous sedation, breathing problems, falls, and accidents. This combination can be life-threatening, especially if opioids or other sedatives are involved.

faqs.q: Is chlordiazepoxide safe for older adults?
faqs.a: Older adults are more sensitive to benzodiazepines and clear them more slowly. Even modest doses can cause confusion, excessive drowsiness, falls, fractures, and thinking problems. Most guidelines recommend avoiding long-acting benzodiazepines like chlordiazepoxide in older adults unless there is a strong and specific reason, such as alcohol withdrawal, and even then, very careful dosing and monitoring are needed.

faqs.q: What happens if I stop chlordiazepoxide suddenly?
faqs.a: If you’ve been taking chlordiazepoxide regularly, stopping abruptly can trigger withdrawal symptoms like anxiety, restlessness, shaking, sweating, trouble sleeping, mood changes, and in severe cases, hallucinations or seizures. These can be dangerous. Always speak with your prescriber before stopping the medication so they can help you taper the dose safely.

seo.description: Learn how chlordiazepoxide (Librium) is used for alcohol withdrawal and short-term anxiety, plus important information about addiction, withdrawal, side effects, and safe use.

metadata.notes: Considered a long-acting benzodiazepine due to long half-life of parent drug and active metabolites.
Often used in inpatient or structured outpatient settings for alcohol withdrawal.
